title: CE-MoE: Fewer Expert Layers, Same Loss, a Third Less Compute
hook: Interleaving an MoE layer after every attention block means paying all-to-all communication over and over. Concentrating experts in a few layers cut GPU-hours by a third at matched quality.
key_points: In expert-parallel MoE training, the all-to-all dispatch and combine collectives can eat a large share of end-to-end training time.
CE-MoE decouples token-mixing depth from channel-mixing depth instead of alternating them one-for-one.
Expert capacity is concentrated in a few routed MoE layers; depth is restored with extra token-mixing and dense-FFN layers.
Tested on a scaling ladder from 2B to 31.5B total parameters at matched total and activated parameter counts.
At 31.5B, the authors report 33.3% fewer GPU-hours plus better average downstream score and inference throughput.
content_html: Mixture-of-Experts models are usually built by dropping an MoE layer after every token-mixing layer — after each attention or Mamba-2 block. Train that with expert parallelism and every one of those layers pays for an all-to-all round trip to dispatch tokens to their experts and combine the results. Sun and Waleffe show that collective can eat a substantial fraction of end-to-end training time, and ask whether the one-for-one interleaving is necessary.
extra_html:
The reconfiguration

CE-MoE decouples token-mixing depth from channel-mixing depth. Expert capacity is concentrated into a few routed MoE layers instead of being spread across all of them, and the depth that removal costs is added back with ordinary token-mixing and dense-FFN layers. Fewer MoE layers means fewer all-to-all collectives, while total and activated parameter counts stay matched to the baseline.

What they measured

Across a scaling ladder from 2B to 31.5B total parameters, CE-MoE models matched validation loss and downstream benchmarks at lower training cost. At 31.5B the authors report 33.3% fewer GPU-hours alongside a better average downstream score and higher inference throughput. See the paper for the layer patterns and the full ladder.

related.hook: Instead of running every input through one big network, route each token to a few specialist sub-networks - total capacity grows without proportional compute.

related.title: Switch Transformer: Scaling to Trillion-Parameter Models
related.hook: Route every token to exactly one expert instead of many - this single simplification made trillion-parameter MoE models stable enough to train at scale.

related.title: Compute-Efficient Hyperparameter Transfer for Large MoEs
related.hook: Sweeping learning rates at trillion-token scale is unaffordable. Transfer across width with muP, then extrapolate along tokens with a fitted scaling law — and trust it for the real run.

flashcards.prompt: What communication cost does expert parallelism add to MoE training?
flashcards.back_html: All-to-all collectives that dispatch tokens to their experts and combine the results — which can consume a substantial fraction of end-to-end training time.

flashcards.prompt: How does CE-MoE keep model depth while using fewer MoE layers?

choices.text: It adds extra token-mixing and dense-FFN layers around the few routed MoE layers
It increases the number of experts activated per token
It replicates each MoE layer's weights across every GPU

flashcards.explanation_html: Depth and expert capacity are decoupled: experts concentrate in a few layers, and plain layers make up the rest of the depth.

flashcards.prompt: What was the headline saving at the 31.5B-parameter scale?
flashcards.back_html: 33.3% fewer GPU-hours than the full-MoE baseline, while matching validation loss and improving average downstream score and inference throughput.
